feedback: If the learner leaves the stages as a straight line: ask 'where does the last step — warming increases — lead?' and have them draw the return arrow from 'warming increases' back to 'ice melts', showing the cycle feeds itself rather than ending.

If the learner sorts a floating sea-ice statement into 'raises sea level': remind them floating ice already displaces its own weight (Archimedes), so only land-ice melt (Greenland/Antarctic sheets) adds water to the sea.

A correct sort or ordering shows the learner can recognise and arrange the loop structure; follow it by asking them to explain in their own words why the loop accelerates, since the sort alone does not elicit that explanation.
activities.intendedInsight: Assembling the cycle shows that the final step loops back to the first, which is what distinguishes a feedback loop from a one-off change.
learnerActions: Lay out the stages of the ice-albedo loop — bright ice reflects sunlight; ice melts; dark ocean is exposed; more heat is absorbed; warming increases — and arrange them into a closed circle rather than a straight line
Draw the return arrow from 'warming increases' back to 'ice melts' to show the cycle feeds itself
Repeat for the permafrost-carbon loop: thaw → methane/CO2 released → more warming → more thaw
Sort statements into 'raises sea level' (land-ice melt) and 'barely changes sea level' (floating sea-ice melt)
activities.title: Build the loop from parts (label and order the cycle)

feedback: If the learner lists facts without closing the loop ('dark water absorbs heat, ice is shrinking, permafrost thaws'): ask them to connect each step to the next and back to the start.

For the 'stayed white' question: if the surface stayed bright and kept reflecting sunlight, the extra absorbed-heat step disappears, so the ice-albedo loop would no longer amplify the melting — some melting would still happen from greenhouse warming, but less. This shows albedo is what drives this particular loop.
If the learner says 'it's too late': redirect to the emissions idea — the pace depends on human greenhouse-gas choices.
activities.intendedInsight: Producing a spoken cause-and-effect explanation forces the learner to close the causal circle and transfer the loop idea to a new case, rather than listing facts.
learnerActions: In your own words, explain to a listener why Arctic sea ice loss is bigger than warming alone would cause — say what happens AND why the loop makes the change bigger
Add permafrost thaw as a second reinforcing loop in your explanation
Answer a probing follow-up: 'Is there anything that would make it slow down on its own, or does the loop only push one way?'
Answer: 'What if the ocean under the ice had somehow stayed white — would the melting still speed up?' and justify your answer
activities.title: Explain it like a climate scientist

feedback: If the learner points only to one dip: highlight the multi-decade downward slope beneath the year-to-year variation.
Anchor the figure: the September minimum is declining about 12–13% per decade relative to the 1981–2010 average over the satellite record (the verified NASA value is ~12.2%).
activities.intendedInsight: The downward trend is evidenced by measured data, not asserted; a long record distinguishes a real decline from year-to-year wobble.
learnerActions: Study an Arctic September sea-ice extent graph covering the satellite record (since 1979) and describe the trend in your own words
State roughly how fast the September minimum is falling per decade and explain how you read it from the graph
Answer: 'What's your evidence that the ice is really shrinking, not just moving around from year to year?'
activities.title: Read the evidence: sea-ice extent over time
